claims.text: Reducing oxygen and nitrogen impurities during processing will improve the high-temperature mechanical capability of TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy.
Reducing oxygen and nitrogen will not compromise room-temperature strength or ductility.
Reducing oxygen and nitrogen will not increase alloy density.
TiVNbTa undergoes age softening during thermal exposure at 700°C.
The age softening of TiVNbTa is associated with interstitial-impurity-driven phase segregation.
Improved vacuum conditions and/or inert-gas shielding will significantly reduce oxygen and nitrogen incorporation during alloy synthesis.
The impurity-control intervention will be effective during aging at 700°C.
Aging at 700°C mimics jet-turbine operating temperatures.
Lower interstitial content will stabilize the solid-solution microstructure by reducing impurity-driven phase segregation.
Lower interstitial content will reduce depletion of strengthening solute interstitials from the metal matrix during aging.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen initially contribute to solid-solution strengthening in TiVNbTa.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen promote phase segregation during thermal aging.
Depletion of solute interstitials from the matrix produces progressive softening with aging time.
Starting with lower oxygen and nitrogen levels will preserve solid-solution strengthening at elevated temperature.
The impurity-controlled alloy will have higher high-temperature yield strength and less time-dependent softening than the standard-processed baseline.
The impurity-controlled alloy will retain room-temperature strength and ductility relative to the baseline.
The density will remain nearly unchanged because oxygen and nitrogen are present only at trace levels.
Standard-processed TiVNbTa containing higher trace oxygen and nitrogen is an appropriate baseline for the proposed low-impurity material.
The intervention may fail unless impurities are reduced below a critical threshold.
Processing-induced changes in grain structure or other microstructural features could independently affect mechanical properties.
